opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is just being really comfortable with a particular style of mathematical and theoretical work, where the problem isn't well-posed yet. A lot of what we're doing is trying to figure out what the right question even is. We're asking things like: what would it mean to have a reasonable estimate of some quantity in a neural network, or an explanation for why a model behaves the way it does, when we don't have a formal definition of "explanation" to start from? So you need people who can live in that ambiguity and still make concrete progress, people who can propose a definition, find the counterexample that breaks it, and iterate.

In practice that means a strong math or theoretical CS background helps a lot. People who've done research in areas like complexity theory, probability, or logic tend to have the right instincts, because they're used to thinking carefully about what can and can't be computed efficiently, and about what it means for an argument to be valid versus just plausible. But the background matters less than the taste. I care about whether someone can tell the difference between a problem that's hard because it's deep and one that's hard because it's been set up badly.

The other thing I look for is a willingness to engage with the motivating problem. This isn't pure math for its own sake. We're trying to get a handle on cases where an AI system might behave badly for reasons we can't see from its training behavior. So it's valuable when someone keeps asking, "Okay, but if we had this, would it actually help with the alignment problem?" That keeps the work honest. It's easy to drift into something elegant that doesn't bear on what we care about.

And honestly, a certain kind of patience. This is a long-shot research bet. Most of the time you're stuck, and the ideas that seem promising fall apart when you look closely. You need people who find that process fun rather than demoralizing, and who are excited by the possibility that if this works, it could be a really big deal for making AI systems safe.

r001.rationale: The response names willingness to engage with the alignment problem and patience with a long-shot, often-stalled research effort as desired collaborator traits.

r002.rationale: It does not identify a lack of compelling examples as the sole reason the project is not obviously attractive.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the heuristic estimator work is a somewhat strange kind of research, and that shapes a lot of what we're looking for. It's not really empirical ML, and it's not quite mainstream theoretical computer science either. We're trying to formalize what it means to have a defeasible, informal argument about why a neural network behaves the way it does, and then ask whether you can build an algorithm that produces estimates from those arguments in a principled way. That's a weird target, so the first thing we care about is whether someone can actually get traction on an ill-defined problem rather than needing someone to hand them a clean conjecture.

Concretely, a lot of the people who have been most useful are people with a mathematical background, often from complexity theory or probability or something adjacent, who are comfortable spending a long time in a state where the definitions keep moving under them. A lot of the work is iterating on what the right formal object even is. You write down a candidate notion of what a heuristic argument is, you try to prove things about it, you find a counterexample that breaks it, and then you have to decide whether the counterexample reveals something deep or whether you just wrote the definition down slightly wrong. Someone who finds that process energizing rather than demoralizing is a big deal.

The second thing is taste about which toy problems matter. We spend a lot of time on very simple cases, like estimating the probability that a boolean circuit outputs one, or understanding the behavior of a small model on a specific distribution. It's easy to either go too abstract and lose contact with the thing we actually care about, or go too concrete and end up solving a special case that doesn't generalize. The people who do well are the ones who can hold the eventual alignment motivation in their head while working on something that looks on the surface like a pure math exercise, and who have good instincts about when a simplification has thrown away the hard part.

Third, and this is maybe underrated, I look for people who are willing to be wrong in public inside the group. A lot of the progress we've made has come from someone saying "I think this approach is doomed because of X" and then us figuring out whether X is real. If people are too cautious about stating strong claims, the discussion gets slow. So I like collaborators who will commit to a position and then update quickly when the evidence comes in.

And then there's the obvious stuff. It helps a lot if someone cares about the alignment problem for its own sake, because the payoff timeline here is long and uncertain, and if the main thing motivating you is publishing or prestige, this is probably not the best place to be. But I'd also say we don't need people to already be steeped in alignment discourse. Some of the best contributions have come from people who hadn't thought much about AI at all but who were just very good at thinking clearly about proof systems or about what it means for a claim to be justified. The translation from that skill set to our problem has turned out to be shorter than I expected.

r001.rationale: The response says collaborators should care about alignment for its own sake because the payoff timeline is long and uncertain, supporting motivation through difficult, prolonged work.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify lack of compelling examples as the sole reason the project is not obviously attractive; it describes several other challenges and traits.

astra-6.text:
I think the main thing is finding people who are excited about making the underlying ideas precise. The heuristic estimator project is fairly speculative. You’re trying to formalize what it means to make reasonable guesses about the outputs of computations without actually running those computations, and then have those guesses fit together in a coherent way.

So I’m especially interested in people with good mathematical taste, who can move between an informal intuition and a concrete toy problem. Can you take a property we think an estimator ought to satisfy, work through some examples, and discover that it’s impossible—or that it has some surprising consequence? Being willing to spend time on that kind of question seems pretty important.

You don’t necessarily need a lot of background in alignment. I’d be more excited about someone who understands the problem, has independent ideas about how to attack it, and can explain where they think my intuitions are wrong.

r001.rationale: The response values precision, mathematical taste, and independent ideas, but does not identify alignment motivation as a trait that sustains work through difficulty.

r002.rationale: It calls the project speculative, but does not say that a lack of compelling examples is the sole reason it is not obviously attractive to work on.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main thing I’d look for is someone who can take a somewhat vague idea and make it precise without losing the thing you were interested in. There’s a lot of back and forth between asking, “What should a heuristic estimator do?” and then trying to write down a definition and discovering that it has some very silly consequence.

So mathematical strength is useful, but I’m especially excited about people who generate their own examples and counterexamples. If I propose a definition, I want someone who will say, “Here’s a case where that gives the wrong answer,” or, “Here’s a simpler problem that seems to capture the difficulty.” That’s often more valuable than being able to prove a hard theorem once the problem is already well specified.

And then there’s a question of independent judgment. You need to be willing to spend time understanding why I think an approach is promising, but also willing to conclude that it’s confused. The ideal collaboration is one where we can disagree about something, make the disagreement concrete, and actually learn from it.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes precision, mathematical strength, generating examples and counterexamples, and independent judgment. It does not identify alignment motivation sufficient to sustain difficult work as a desired trait.

r002.rationale: The response discusses using examples and counterexamples to assess definitions, but does not say that a lack of compelling examples is the sole reason the project is not obviously attractive to work on.
